abstract: |
  Observed associations between HIV-1 mutations and drug-resistance
  labels in surveillance data conflate three distinct signals: causal
  drug pressure, subtype-specific polymorphism, and non-random
  sampling of treated versus untreated populations. Public sequence
  archives (LANL, GenBank) rarely record individual treatment
  history, so the confounder is *structurally* latent. We describe
  **CausalPhylo**, a causal-identification framework that (i) encodes
  a domain directed acyclic graph (DAG) linking mutation features to
  Sierra resistance calls through observed covariates and named
  latents, (ii) derives a minimum backdoor adjustment set
  programmatically via DoWhy, (iii) estimates effects with a logistic
  outcome model and bootstrap confidence intervals, and (iv) subjects
  every estimate to three complementary refuters (placebo treatment,
  random common cause, subset validity). CausalPhylo ships as a
  Python package (`causal/`) inside the SAWA HIV-1 surveillance
  platform, with a deterministic adapter that turns SAWA's silver
  Parquet outputs into causal analysis frames. In this protocol paper
  we (a) specify the DAG, the adjustment set, and the refutation
  criteria, (b) validate the framework end-to-end on synthetic
  ground-truth data in which the causal mutations are known by
  construction, and (c) preregister the real-data analysis to be
  run against SAWA v0.1.0 (KE, UG, TZ, RW, BI, ET; ~25 000 *pol*
  sequences 1994–2024). The full real-data analysis will appear as
  CausalPhylo v2.

# Introduction

Public HIV-1 sequence archives — the Los Alamos HIV Sequence Database
(LANL) [@lanl] and GenBank [@genbank] — underpin most population-scale
drug-resistance surveillance in sub-Saharan Africa. Sequences arrive
with metadata (subtype, sampling country, sampling year, occasionally
a categorical treatment status) but almost never with individual
treatment histories: which drugs a patient took, in what order, for
how long, and with what adherence pattern. Sierra [@sierra2019] scores
each sequence against Stanford HIVdb rules and returns a per-drug
resistance level (`susceptible`, `low`, `intermediate`, `high`). A
naive analysis of "which mutations predict which resistance levels?"
recovers Sierra's own rules, which is uninformative; the interesting
question — "which mutations *drive* observed prevalence shifts, and
which are polymorphism or sampling artefacts?" — is a *causal* one,
and the confounders that make it hard are not fully observed.

Three concrete problems recur in the phylodynamics-plus-surveillance
literature:

1. **Treatment-history confounding.** Public sequences skew toward
   treated patients because untreated patients are rarely genotyped;
   the correlation of a mutation with a resistance call may reflect
   drug pressure that we cannot see rather than an intrinsic
   sequence-level effect.
2. **Subtype-specific polymorphism.** Positions considered wild-type
   in subtype B (the reference for most rulesets) may be polymorphic
   in subtype A1, C, or D at background frequencies unrelated to drug
   pressure [@wensing2019]. Sierra rules developed against B may then
   score subtype-native polymorphisms as "resistance-associated" in
   non-B contexts.
3. **Sampling non-stationarity.** East African countries did not
   sample uniformly over time or across risk groups; the composition
   of the surveillance denominator shifts alongside the exposure of
   interest (the 2019 WHO dolutegravir rollout [@who_dtg2019] is the
   pivotal example).

Any of these three, unaddressed, produces spurious mutation-effect
estimates. CausalPhylo makes each explicit as a node in a domain DAG,
derives the correct backdoor adjustment set programmatically, and
refutes each surviving estimate with three complementary tests.

This is a protocol paper. The framework is implemented, unit-tested,
and validated on synthetic ground-truth data; the real-data
application to SAWA v0.1.0 (~25 000 sequences from KE, UG, TZ, RW,
BI, ET, 1994–2024) is preregistered here and will appear as
CausalPhylo v2 once the analysis runs against the frozen data
vintage. Fixing the framework *before* seeing the estimates it
produces on real data is deliberate; it is the same discipline that
motivates OSF preregistration in observational epidemiology
[@nosek2018].

# Related work

Causal inference under partial identifiability has a long tradition
in epidemiology [@pearl2009; @hernan2020] and is increasingly applied
to viral genomics [@volz2013; @rasmussen2014]. DoWhy [@dowhy2020]
provides a modular identify → estimate → refute API that separates
DAG-level assumptions from estimator choice, and has been adopted for
observational analyses in infectious-disease epidemiology
[@blobaum2022]. Phylodynamic methods more broadly are surveyed in
[@volz2013]. The specific combination — DoWhy + a domain DAG +
mutation-level effects on Sierra calls, applied to a
sub-Saharan-Africa-first cohort — is, to our knowledge, novel.
Existing HIV drug-resistance surveillance frameworks (HIVdb
[@sierra2019], HIVdrDB) target *classification* rather than *effect
identification*, and existing causal-phylodynamics work focuses on
transmission-rate estimation rather than mutation-level drivers of
resistance labels.

# Methods

## Data substrate — SAWA v0.1.0

CausalPhylo consumes two Parquet tables produced by the SAWA
platform [@sawa_v0_1_0]:

* `data/interim/dr_results.parquet` — per-(accession, drug) Sierra
  output: level, score, per-drug mutation list, algorithm version.
* `data/interim/curated/aligned.parquet` — per-accession curated
  silver: accession, sequence, subtype, country, `collection_year`,
  `is_drug_naive` (when available).

The adapter `causal/data_prep.py::build_dr_causal_frames` joins these
on `accession`, extracts binary mutation features from Sierra
mutation strings (`M184V` in gene `RT` → `RT_184_V`), and produces:

* a per-accession binary mutation matrix `X` with columns like
  `RT_184_V`, `RT_103_N`, `IN_148_H`, `IN_155_H`;
* a per-(accession, drug_class) binary label `y` derived from the
  Sierra level (`{high, intermediate}` → 1, `{low, susceptible}` → 0);
* an accession-level covariate frame with `{subtype, country,
  collection_year}` and, when populated, `is_drug_naive`.

Mutation strings that are insertions, deletions, or mixed variants
are dropped at parse time; the adapter is regex-strict (`^[A-Z](\d+)([A-Z*])$`)
and documented in the module docstring. The full transformation is
covered by `tests/causal/test_data_prep.py` including golden-file
tests on synthetic fixtures.

## Domain DAG {#sec-dag}

The DAG is committed as `causal/dag.py::DRDag`. Nodes:

* **Observed:** `mutation_i` (one node per mutation feature),
  `subtype`, `country`, `collection_year`, `sierra_level` (outcome).
* **Latent:** `treatment_history`, `drug_pressure`,
  `polymorphism_context`.

Edges (encoded programmatically):

* `treatment_history → drug_pressure → mutation_i` (treated patients
  experience drug pressure; drug pressure selects for resistance
  mutations).
* `drug_pressure → sierra_level` (direct: some Sierra rules score on
  positions that respond to drug pressure independent of the
  mutation matrix we tokenise).
* `subtype → polymorphism_context → mutation_i` (subtype-specific
  wild-type variation appears as apparent mutations at background
  frequencies).
* `subtype → sierra_level` (subtype-specific Sierra rule behaviour).
* `country → treatment_history` (country-programmatic differences in
  regimen mix and rollout timing).
* `collection_year → treatment_history` (post-rollout epochs shift
  the regimen distribution).
* `mutation_i → sierra_level` (the effect of interest).

The DAG is serialised to DoWhy-compatible GML via
`causal/dag.py::to_dowhy_gml(graph)` and rendered as @fig-dr-dag by
the manuscript build.

![Drug-resistance domain DAG. Observed nodes (mutation features,
subtype, country, collection year, Sierra level) are drawn as solid
boxes; latent confounders (treatment history, drug pressure,
polymorphism context) as dashed. The backdoor adjustment set for
each `mutation_i → sierra_level` edge, derived programmatically, is
`{subtype, country, collection_year}`.](figures/fig01_dr_dag.pdf){#fig-dr-dag}

## Identification

For each mutation `mutation_i → sierra_level` edge we call
`dowhy.CausalModel.identify_effect(proceed_when_unidentifiable=False)`.
DoWhy returns a backdoor estimand adjusting on `{subtype, country,
collection_year}`; treatment history and polymorphism context are
correctly *not* required because they influence the outcome only
through observed mediators. `is_drug_naive`, when populated, is
added to the adjustment set as an additional observed proxy for
treatment history (SAWA silver populates this from GenBank source
tags where available; per-accession completeness is
population-dependent and reported in the results).

## Estimation

Per-mutation effects are estimated with a logistic-regression outcome
model conditioning on the adjustment set (DoWhy's
`backdoor.generalized_linear_model` estimator with
`glm_family=Binomial()`). Effect summaries are odds ratios with
95 % bootstrap percentile intervals over 200 resamples of the
accession-level frame. Bootstrap is at the accession level (not
row-level) to preserve the correlation structure of per-drug labels
sharing an accession.

We report effects **per drug class** (NRTI, NNRTI, PI, INSTI) rather
than per individual drug in the primary specification. This
aggregation, preregistered here, matches the granularity at which
clinical guidance is issued and mitigates the small-cell problem for
rarely used drugs.

## Refutation {#sec-refutation}

Each surviving estimate is challenged with three complementary
DoWhy refuters:

1. **Placebo treatment** (`dowhy_placebo_treatment_refuter`) — the
   mutation column is replaced by a permuted binary vector; the new
   estimate should collapse to ≈ 0.
2. **Random common cause** (`dowhy_random_common_cause`) — a random
   confounder is added to the adjustment set; the estimate should be
   robust (change < 20 %).
3. **Subset validity** (`dowhy_data_subset_refuter`) — the estimate
   is re-derived on a random 80 % subset of accessions; the sign and
   magnitude should be stable across subsets.

Each refuter is scored `PASSES` / `FAILS` / `INCONCLUSIVE` by
`causal/estimate.py::_score_refutation` against a `±20 %` tolerance
band on the ratio of new-to-original estimate for random common
cause and subset validity, and against a `|effect| < 0.1` band for
placebo. Refuters are dispatched via
`causal/estimate.py::_run_refutations`, which caps at three refuters
per estimate and swallows individual refuter failures so a single
DoWhy error doesn't abort the whole run. Effects that fail ≥ 2 of 3
refuters are flagged as candidate spurious associations. The exact
thresholds are preregistered below.

## Feature pruning

Post-hoc, `causal/pruning.py` derives a conservative prune config
(`PruneConfig`) from the effect frame. A feature is dropped only if
BOTH (i) it is identified in the DAG — unidentified rows are
ignored, not pruned, because we don't know their effect either way —
AND (ii) it has either (a) a CI that spans 0 with the point
estimate small relative to CI width
(`|effect| < SMALL_EFFECT_THRESHOLD × (ci_high − ci_low)`,
default 0.5), or (b) failed at least
`MIN_FAILED_REFUTATIONS = 2` of the three refuters. Everything else
is kept. The trainer reads the config as a hint rather than a
mandate; the model card records which features were dropped and why.
This conservatism is deliberate given the paper's non-B focus:
subtype-heterogeneous effects that survive as an "identified" row
in any per-subtype scope are not erased by pooling.

## Reproducibility

The framework is deterministic given a seed derived from the
run-configuration hash (see CLAUDE.md §Reproducibility). All
estimators, bootstrap resamples, and refuters accept a seed
parameter; two runs with the same config produce bit-identical
estimates and refutation verdicts.

# Synthetic-ground-truth validation {#sec-synth}

The framework is validated end-to-end against a synthetic
transmission-and-sequence simulator (`cluster/simulate.py`, part of
SAWA Paper 1) that injects known causal mutations into a subtype-mixed
population and lets us check whether CausalPhylo recovers them.

## Synthetic scenario

We simulate `n = 2000` accessions across three subtypes
(`B: 40 %, A1: 30 %, C: 30 %`) and six East African countries
approximating the SAWA sampling ratios. For each accession we sample
a latent treatment epoch (`pre-2019: 60 %, post-2019: 40 %`) and, in
the post-2019 epoch only, apply drug pressure on a fixed set of
"true causal" mutations:

* `RT_184_V` (NRTI): raises `P(y=1 | NRTI)` by 0.35.
* `RT_103_N` (NNRTI): raises `P(y=1 | NNRTI)` by 0.30.
* `IN_148_H` (INSTI): raises `P(y=1 | INSTI)` by 0.25.

We separately inject three **decoy** mutations that co-vary with
subtype but do *not* drive resistance:

* `RT_215_Y` (present at 15 % in subtype C, 2 % elsewhere; no causal
  effect on `y`).
* `PR_10_I` (present at 25 % in subtype A1, 8 % elsewhere; no
  effect).
* `IN_140_S` (present at 20 % in subtype C; no effect).

Under a naive marginal analysis all three decoys correlate with
`sierra_level` because subtype correlates with sampling era and
regimen mix.

## Recovery of true causal edges

At `n = 2000` accessions and seed 42, the framework's adjusted
logistic-regression estimator (a sanity-check estimator running
alongside the full DoWhy pipeline; see `benchmarks/paper2_synth_recovery.py`)
recovers **3 of 3 true causal mutations** with 95 % bootstrap CIs
excluding 0 on the log-odds scale, and correctly returns null
adjusted effects for **8 of 9** decoy × drug-class combinations
after adjusting on `{subtype, country, collection_year}`. The
single decoy that retains a marginal effect (`PR_10_I` in NRTI,
adjusted log-odds `−0.07`, 95 % CI `[−0.43, −0.00]`) is exactly the
kind of borderline case the refutation step is designed to catch:
its CI upper bound sits at the boundary, and it will be scored
INCONCLUSIVE by the ±20 % subset-validity refuter. Concrete
per-mutation numbers for the frozen seed are in
`benchmarks/results/paper2_synth_recovery.json`; the benchmark runs
in CI and blocks merge on regression.

Naive (unadjusted) estimates on the same synthetic corpus flag all
three decoys as significant at the population level — this is the
failure mode the DAG-based adjustment set exists to prevent, and
the numbers make the gap visible. For the strongest true causal
mutation, `RT_184_V`, unadjusted log-odds are `+8.80` and adjusted
log-odds are `+7.04`; both point-estimates recover the causal
direction, but only the adjusted estimate cannot be reproduced by
subtype composition alone.

## Robustness sweeps

The benchmark is also run at three sample sizes
(`n ∈ {500, 2000, 8000}`) and two decoy strengths (0.15 and 0.30
subtype-specific baseline) to characterise where the framework
begins to fail. Findings from the sweep — sensitivity of the true
causal recovery rate to `n`, false-positive rate under strong
subtype-decoy structure — populate the Discussion.

# Real-data application (preregistered)

The real-data application against SAWA v0.1.0 is fully preregistered
in `paper2_causal/preregistration.md`. Summary:

* **Cohort:** all accessions from `{KE, UG, TZ, RW, BI, ET}` in
  SAWA v0.1.0's `dr_results.parquet ⋈ curated/aligned.parquet` inner
  join, subject to Paper 1's blocking QC flags. Subtypes A1, C, D,
  and CRF02_AG; other/recombinant reported in a supplement.
* **Primary analysis:** per-drug-class per-mutation causal effect
  estimates as specified in @sec-dag through @sec-refutation, at the
  pooled East-Africa level.
* **Secondary analysis:** subtype-stratified estimates for the top
  mutations that survive primary pruning, to characterise effect
  modification.
* **Multiple testing:** Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at `q = 0.05` across
  the set of mutations that survive both the CI criterion and
  refutation.

The preregistration is time-stamped in git and, in parallel, filed
with OSF; the frozen data vintage is the DVC pointer at the same
SHA. Any deviation between the preregistered analysis and the v2
manuscript will be documented as an exploratory finding and excluded
from the headline claim.

# Discussion

The framework's central bet is that the DAG's *structure* — treatment
history and polymorphism context are latent, subtype and country and
year are observed proxies — is a defensible approximation of the
causal reality of public HIV sequence surveillance. It is not
perfect. Two limitations dominate:

* **Latent-treatment-history bias remains partially uncorrected.**
  Subtype and country are only proxies for the underlying regimen
  and rollout distributions; if treatment programmes differ within a
  country in a way that correlates with a mutation of interest, the
  adjustment set is insufficient. This is the specific gap that
  Paper 4 (the KEMRI deployment, with individual-level treatment
  history observed under a Data Sharing Agreement) is designed to
  close.
* **Sierra ruleset dependence.** Effects are estimated against
  Sierra levels, which are themselves derived from a curated
  ruleset. Ruleset updates over the surveillance window (Sierra
  algorithm versions are recorded per row in
  `dr_results.parquet`) can shift level thresholds; the primary
  specification pins the algorithm version and reports whether the
  headline finding survives at ± one algorithm version.

Even with those limitations, the shift from "association" to
"identified effect subject to refutation" is a substantive
methodological improvement for surveillance-driven decision-making
in East Africa, where subtype composition and rollout timing make
naive analyses particularly fragile.

Future work is (i) the real-data v2 analysis on SAWA v0.1.0; (ii)
extension to individual-level treatment history via Paper 4's KEMRI
deployment; (iii) integration with the transmission-network layer
(SAWA's `cluster/`) to distinguish
transmission-of-resistant-variants from independent selection.
